title: Triple fiducia (future / present / past remission) — dispositive, formal, consolatory
source_text: CVI. Ut autem explicent quomodo nihilominus fiducia illa, quae promissiones gratiae credenti cuique sigillatim applicat, sit actus ille per quem justificamur, in fiducia ista triplicem actum distinguunt, ut verbis eorum supra exposuimus. Primus actus est quo credimus in futuro, peccata nobis esse remittenda: secundus, quo in praesenti credimus, peccata nobis remitti: tertius, quo credimus in praeterito peccata jam esse remissa. Per primum actum, juxta illos, homo disponitur quidem ad justificationem, sed donec in eo haeret, nondum est justificatus; per secundum accipit remissionem peccatorum, & actu justificatur; per tertium percipit & sentit jam factam justificationem; unde oritur ejus consolatio. Unde est quod dicunt primum actum esse dispositorium ad justificationem, secundum formaliter justificatorium, & tertium consolatorium. Quae ratio videtur, cur dicant illum esse in fide praecipuum, quia ad fidelium animarum consolationem maxime & proxime facit.
pass_a_gloss: But so that they may explain how nevertheless that trust which applies the promises of grace to each believer one by one is the act by which we are justified, they distinguish in that trust a threefold act, as we set out above in their words. The first act is that by which we believe for the future that sins are to be remitted to us; the second, by which in the present we believe sins are being remitted to us; the third, by which we believe in the past that sins have already been remitted. By the first act, according to them, a person is indeed disposed toward justification, but while he remains in it he is not yet justified; by the second he receives remission of sins and is actually justified; by the third he perceives and feels justification already done, whence his consolation arises. Hence they say the first act is dispositive toward justification, the second formally justificatory, and the third consolatory. Which reason seems why they call that one chief in faith, because it most and most nearly serves the consolation of the faithful.
pass_b_english: To save calling applying-fiducia the justifying act, some distinguish three moments in it: future (sins will be remitted), present (sins are being remitted), past (sins already remitted).
On their scheme: first only disposes; second formally justifies; third consoles by sensing justification done.
They call the consolatory sense “chief” because it most immediately comforts the faithful.
